{{more citations needed|date=February 2016}}

The '''Jones–Dole equation''', or Jones–Dole expression, is an empirical expression that describes the relationship between the [[viscosity]] of a [[Solution (chemistry)|solution]] and the concentration of solute within the solution (at a fixed temperature and pressure).<ref>{{Cite web | title=School of Chemistry {{!}} University of Leicester | url=http://www.le.ac.uk/chemistry/thermodynamics/pdfs/3000/Topic2930.pdf | access-date=2026-01-01 | website=www.le.ac.uk}}</ref> The Jones–Dole equation is written as<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Jones |first1=Grinnell |last2=Dole |first2=Malcolm |title=The Viscosity of Aqueous Solutions of Strong Electrolytes with Special Reference to Barium Chloride |date=1929-10-01 |journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society |volume=51 |issue=10 |pages=2950–2964 |doi=10.1021/ja01385a012 |bibcode=1929JAChS..51.2950J |issn=0002-7863}}</ref>
<math display="block">\frac{\eta}{\eta_0} = 1 + A C^\frac{1}{2} + B C,</math>
where
: ''η'' is the viscosity of the solution (at a fixed temperature and pressure),
: ''η''<sub>0</sub> is the viscosity of the solvent at the same temperature and pressure,
: ''A'' is a [[coefficient]] that describes the impact of charge–charge interactions on the viscosity of a solution (it is usually positive) and can be calculated from [[Debye–Hückel theory]],
: ''B'' is a coefficient that characterises the solute–solvent interactions at a defined temperature and pressure,
: ''C'' is the solute concentration.

The Jones–Dole ''B'' coefficient<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Jenkins |first1=H. Donald B. |last2=Marcus |first2=Yizhak |date=1995-12-01 |title=Viscosity B-Coefficients of Ions in Solution |journal=Chemical Reviews |volume=95 |issue=8 |pages=2695–2724 |doi=10.1021/cr00040a004 |issn=0009-2665}}</ref> is often used to classify ions as either structure-makers (kosmotropes) or structure-breakers ([[chaotrope]]s) according to their supposed strengthening or weakening of the [[Hydrogen bond#Water|hydrogen-bond network of water]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Marcus |first=Yizhak |date=2009-03-11 |title=Effect of Ions on the Structure of Water: Structure Making and Breaking |journal=Chemical Reviews |volume=109 |issue=3 |pages=1346–1370 |doi=10.1021/cr8003828 |issn=0009-2665 |pmid=19236019}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ball |first1=Philip |last2=Hallsworth |first2=John E. |date=2015-03-23 |title=Water structure and chaotropicity: their uses, abuses and biological implications |url=http://xlink.rsc.org/?DOI=C4CP04564E |journal=Physical Chemistry Chemical Physics |language=en |volume=17 |issue=13 |pages=8297–8305 |doi=10.1039/c4cp04564e |pmid=25628033 |bibcode=2015PCCP...17.8297B |issn=1463-9084|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The Jones–Dole expression works well up to about 1&nbsp;M, but at higher concentrations breaks down, as the viscosity of all solutions increase rapidly at high concentrations.

The large increase in viscosity as a function of solute concentration seen in all solutions above about 1&nbsp;M is the effect of a [[Jamming (physics)|jamming]] transition at a high concentration. As a result, the viscosity increases exponentially as a function of concentration and then diverges at a critical concentration. This has been referred to as the "Mayonnaise effect",<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Wynne |first=Klaas |date=2017-12-08 |title=The Mayonnaise Effect |journal=The Journal of Physical Chemistry Letters |volume=8 |issue=24 |pages=6189–6192 |doi=10.1021/acs.jpclett.7b03207 |issn=1948-7185|url=http://eprints.gla.ac.uk/153368/7/153368.pdf |pmid=29220573 }}</ref> as the viscosity of [[mayonnaise]] (essentially a solution of oil in water) is extremely high because of the jamming of micrometer-scale droplets.
